growth_ceiling_reason: a doubling sentinel, not a byte budget. Five growth runs of one unmodified build came back at 192, 384, 422, 461 and 461 first-party bytes per extra visit per host (an earlier batch, divided by the library size read before the visits rather than after, spread 230 to 499). What moves is how many times the page reads the library during a visit and how many hosts discovery had added by then, neither of which this repository controls, so a ceiling at one graph per host per visit -- 384 -- would go red on the shipped code. The ceiling therefore sits above two graphs per visit per host (768, which still passes and is written down as the blind spot in the fixtures) and refuses at three (1152), which is what a second owner of the TemporaryHost/TemporaryApp cycle looks like rather than a busier render.

ci_runner.byte_budget: judged in the seeded runs: 512 per leaked host plus a 128 floor, and both sat inside it (2,688 against 3,712, 2,304 against 3,200). Under the ceiling this file carried until that push, both runs would have been refused -- 24,416 against 19,500 and 23,424 against 17,000 -- which is the change of rule measured on a runner rather than argued at a desk
ci_runner.first_party_classes: none in the two runs before the seed; TemporaryApp and TemporaryHost in the two seeded runs, nothing else

growth.inside_the_laptop_spread: yes: the laptop's five runs were 192, 384, 422, 461 and 461
growth.measured_on: 2026-09-24, run 36000138662, arm64 and x86_64, GitHub macOS runners: our objects went 3,456 to 4,608 bytes on arm64 and 3,456 to 4,992 on x86_64 across 5 extra visits, one host in the library either way, 384 bytes per leaked graph in every sweep
growth.what_the_two_sweeps_recorded: the first sweep of each pair seeded the host (status seeded), the second found one already in the library (status existing-hosts) -- discovery reached the database before the seed check did. Which of the two arrives first is not decided by this repository, which is why the denominator is the library read at the end of the run

total_bytes.why_it_is_not_a_ceiling: the report's total is every leaked object in the process: on the laptop 80% of it was CoreFoundation strings, sets and dictionaries, and a GitHub runner reports ~18.7k of it with not one first-party object among them. Budgeting that against the host count is budgeting the machine
